meta.title: Who really said "An Anecdote Is A Revealing Account of an Incident That Never Occurred in the Life of Some Famous Person"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Bennett Cerf's line. The joke ran unsigned in Life magazine in 1912; Cerf printed the 'revealing' wording in his 1965 column. The author is anonymous.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'An Anecdote Is A Revealing Account of an Incident That Never Occurred in the Life of Some Famous Person'?
meta.ogDescription: Quote Investigator traces this joke to an unsigned 1912 Life lexicon. Bennett Cerf reprinted it in 1965 with one word changed. The creator is anonymous.

answer.label: Not Bennett Cerf — an anonymous joke from 1912
answer.sourceLine: Bennett Cerf really did print this sentence — in his syndicated newspaper column “Try and Stop Me” on 28 October 1965, where he swapped “revealing” in for “brief.” He did not write it. Quote Investigator ↗ traces the joke back through Evan Esar to an unsigned entry in the New York humour weekly Life on 12 September 1912, and concludes that its creator is anonymous.

source.excerpt: Anecdote: A revealing account of an incident that never occurred in the life of some famous person.
trail: 12 September 1912 — the earliest printing anyone has found runs unsigned in “Life’s Lucid Lexicon,” a joke column in the New York humour weekly Life: “Anecdote—A brief account of an incident that never occurred in the life of some famous man.” No author is named. Quote Investigator ↗

1951 — the definition appears on page 24 of the revised and enlarged Esar’s Comic Dictionary, already reading “some famous person” — that half of the shift predates Cerf by fourteen years. Evan Esar takes no credit: his foreword says the book’s contents are of popular origin and therefore unattributed. Quote Investigator ↗

28 October 1965 — Bennett Cerf runs the quip in his syndicated column “Try and Stop Me” in the Reading Eagle, page 18, substituting “revealing” for “brief.” That variant is the one circulating under his name today. Quote Investigator ↗

Cerf’s trade was collecting, not coining. His 1944 best-seller is catalogued as Try and Stop Me: a collection of anecdotes and stories, mostly humorous, with Cerf credited as its compiler. Internet Archive ↗
source.excerptNote: As printed in Bennett Cerf’s syndicated column “Try and Stop Me,” 28 October 1965. Fifty-three years earlier the same joke had run unsigned in the humour weekly Life, two words different: “Anecdote—A brief account of an incident that never occurred in the life of some famous man.”

source.rightsNote: The joke itself is old enough to be free: the 1912 Life printing — “a brief account — some famous man” — was published well before 1931 and is public domain in the United States. This exact wording is not that one. The “revealing…famous person” form is first documented in Bennett Cerf’s syndicated column of 28 October 1965, so the sentence as quoted here should be treated as in copyright. No rightsholder is established: the wording is anonymous in origin, so whatever right subsists in the 1965 column as published would sit with the newspaper syndicate that ran it — not with Cerf, who did not write the line.

author.name: Bennett Cerf
author.heading: Bennett Cerf — anthologist, not author
author.metaLine: 1898–1971 · Random House co-founder, joke anthologist, What's My Line? panelist
author.bio: Bennett Cerf co-founded Random House in 1927 with Donald S. Klopfer and became its best-known public face, but a much larger audience knew him from the television panel show What’s My Line?, on which he appeared from 1951. His fame outside publishing rested on humour: Try and Stop Me (1944), Shake Well Before Using (1948) and a long run of similar collections. Those books were compilations — anecdotes, puns and gags gathered from other people and older printed sources, with Cerf credited on the 1944 volume as its compiler. That is precisely how this definition reached his column, and why his name on it settles nothing about who wrote it.

copyAttribution: "Anecdote: A revealing account of an incident that never occurred in the life of some famous person." — Anonymous. Earliest known printing unsigned in Life (New York), 12 September 1912, as "a brief account of an incident that never occurred in the life of some famous man." Bennett Cerf printed this "revealing" wording in his syndicated column "Try and Stop Me" on 28 October 1965, but did not originate it. Source: Quote Investigator.

misattribution.heading: Three names it gets hung on
misattribution.intro: This is a joke about attributions that never happened, which has spent a century collecting attributions that never happened. All three men most often credited with it printed it; none of them wrote it, and two said so outright.

items.why: Cerf did print this exact sentence, in his syndicated column of 28 October 1965, which is why his name rides with it. But the joke was already fifty-three years old by then, and Cerf’s column was a digest of other people’s material. Quote Investigator ↗

A 1976 article in Mid-South Folklore called it “Evan Esar’s facetious definition,” pointing to his book The Humor of Humor. Esar refused the credit himself: his own dictionary’s foreword states that its contents are of popular origin and therefore unattributed, and in The Humor of Humor he introduces the line as something the Comic Dictionary says. Quote Investigator ↗

The urban-legend scholar quoted the definition in the Deseret News on 6 December 1991, and readers have credited him ever since. He introduced it as the work of “another wit” and never claimed it. Quote Investigator ↗

misattribution.truthLine: Nobody owns it. After following the line from 1991 back to an unsigned 1912 lexicon entry, Quote Investigator ↗ concludes that the creator of this sharp definition remains anonymous — Cerf, Esar and Brunvand were each passing along a joke that had arrived with no name attached.

context.heading: The joke that proves itself
lead: There is a small, perfect irony here. A one-line definition mocking the way anecdotes attach themselves to famous men has spent more than a century attaching itself to famous men. It was born anonymous in a 1912 humour column, drifted through an Australian paper and a London monthly by 1914, got printed in a joke dictionary whose compiler explicitly declined authorship, and finally landed on Bennett Cerf — a man whose entire public reputation was built on repeating other people’s stories.

Cerf is the ideal magnet for it. He co-founded Random House, sat on What’s My Line? for years, and published one best-selling anthology of gags after another. When a quip needs a plausible owner, a professional wit with a syndicated column is the obvious place for it to settle. The 1965 column entry is genuine; the ownership it implies is not.
detailsBody: The line travelled fast and early. Quote Investigator records it in The Windsor Magazine of London in February 1914 and in Sydney’s Sydney Mail that April, under the heading “Some Definitions by a Modern Cynic” — both still without an author.

One edition detail matters if you go looking for it yourself: the entry is in the 1951 revised and enlarged Esar’s Comic Dictionary (Horizon Press, page 24). Quote Investigator notes that the earlier 1943 Harvest House edition has no alphabetical entry for “anecdote” at all.
context.pull: A joke about fake attributions, faked onto a famous name.

sourcesVerified.claim: The earliest known instance is 12 September 1912 in Life (New York), volume 60, issue 1559, page 1774, in "Life's Lucid Lexicon", reading "Anecdote—A brief account of an incident that never occurred in the life of some famous man", with no attribution.
Bennett Cerf included the quip in his syndicated newspaper column "Try and Stop Me" on 28 October 1965 (Reading Eagle, page 18, column 5), using "revealing" instead of "brief".

The definition appears on page 24 of the 1951 revised and enlarged Esar's Comic Dictionary (Horizon Press, New York), and Esar's foreword disclaims authorship, saying the contents are of popular origin and therefore unattributed; the 1943 Harvest House edition has no entry for "anecdote".

A 1976 Mid-South Folklore article called it "Evan Esar's facetious definition" and pointed to The Humor of Humor, page 32; Jan Harold Brunvand quoted it in the Deseret News of 6 December 1991 while crediting only "another wit".
Quote Investigator's stated conclusion is that the creator of this definition remains anonymous.
The joke also appeared in The Windsor Magazine (London) in February 1914 and in the Sydney Mail on 1 April 1914 under "Some Definitions by a Modern Cynic".
Bennett Cerf's 1944 book is titled "Try and stop me, a collection of anecdotes and stories, mostly humorous", published by Simon & Schuster, New York, with Cerf (1898-1971) credited as compiler.
The 1944 book Try and Stop Me is a compilation of anecdotes, urban legends, jokes and profiles of newsmakers, and sold over one million copies in its first two years.

Bennett Cerf was born 25 May 1898 and died 27 August 1971; he co-founded Random House in 1927 with Donald S. Klopfer, wrote humour compilations including Try and Stop Me (1944) and Shake Well Before Using (1948), and was a panelist on What's My Line? beginning in 1951.
Evan Esar (1899-1995) was an American humorist known for witty definitions and for Esar's Comic Dictionary.
The Life magazine of 1912 was an American humor and general-interest weekly published in New York from 1883 to 1936, distinct from the all-photographic Life launched by Henry Luce in 1936.
